(1) the Chinle Group contains four successive microvertebrate faunal assemblages, the Otischalkian (Otis Chalk), Adamanian (Adaman Cliffs), Revueltian and Apachean (both of which are not formally named in this study), and (2) these microvertebrate assem- blages can be used to independently corroborate and extend the existing macroverte- brate biochronology of these deposits.

microvertebrates from the Chinle Group of Arizona and West Texas are useful for biostratigraphically subdividing the Otischalkian through the Revueltian biochrons, but that the Apachean biochron has not yet been sampled in detail.

the Chinle Group contains four biochronologic units, the Otischalkian (late Olenekian), Adamanian (late Anisian to early Ladinian), Revueltian(between early Carnian and early Norian), and the Apachean (late Norian).

developing a biostratigraphical scheme for the Upper Triassic based on microvertebrate fossils.
the distribution and stratigraphic ranges of microvertebrates in the Chinle Group.
the development of microvertebrate biozones and the construction of a microvertebrate chronology of the Chinle Group, which we hope can be extended to the entire lower Mesozoic.

microvertebrate biozones are useful, but the taxa that define them are not.
a microvertebrate assembalge biostratigraphy exists for the Upper Triassic of western North America, but it is not as robust as the macrovertebrate biochronology.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
microvertebrate biozones are possible, and some taxa may be useful for biostratigraphically subdividing the Chinle Group, but the best index fossils for the Upper Triassic are therian mammals.

, although microvertebrates are useful biostratigraphically at the Chinle Group time scale, the most useful taxa are the same ones that have been used in mammal biostratigraphies, and that these taxa are most useful in the Chinle Group because they are so common.

, while microvertebrate taxa have long stratigraphical ranges in the Chinle Group, there is enough variation in the assemblages to construct a biostratigraphy that can be used to complement and extend existing macrovertebrate based biostratigraphy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a robust biostratigraphy based on the distribution and relative abundance of microvertebrate taxa can be constructed for the Upper Triassic.
the microvertebrate fossil record is more complex than the macrovertebrate fossil record and that the former is not merely an extension of the latter.

the Chinle Group is an excellent place to study microvertebrates and that microvertebrates can be used to independently corroborate the existing macrovertebrates-based biostratigraphies of the Triassic.
